title: Pharmaceuticals Stockouts
prompt: A leading pharmaceutical manufacturer is facing frequent stockouts across key domestic markets despite having adequate annual production capacity. The CEO wants you to diagnose the issue and recommend solutions, without investing in new plants.

facts.asks: Is demand strong, and does capacity on paper exceed it

facts.reveal: No, demand is stable and predictable.
Overall inventory is slightly higher than last year.
No. Some SKUs are overstocked, others out of stock.

facts.asks: Are those delays enough to halt high-demand products

facts.reveal: Yes, multiple SKUs run on shared lines.
Why not recommend adding more capacity?

crux.statement: Inventory up yet stockouts means stock is in the wrong place, not short. Forecast drift drives both product-level misallocation under the push model and weekly rescheduling, which means more changeovers on shared lines and lower effective output for fast movers. Single-sourced APIs are the second cause.
crux.clue: "Overall inventory is slightly higher than last year", followed by "some SKUs are overstocked, others out of stock".
crux.test: Remove the inventory rise and the case reads as a supply shortage. Remove the forecast drop and the candidate has no reason for the misallocation.

paths: Demand → supply capacity → distribution (transport, positioning, replenishment logic) → upstream planning (raw materials, schedule stability, yield)

quant.working: Derived: forecast error rose from 100 − 88 = 12% to 100 − 70 = 30%, which is 2.5 times.
quant.answer: Forecast error rose from 12% to 30%, 2.5 times

answerKey: Forecasting: a planning cadence with monthly demand lock-in, product-level analytics for fast movers, frozen production windows
Sourcing: dual sourcing for critical APIs, safety stock for fast movers, secured contracts for the top 20% revenue products
No new capacity: the problem is instability and misallocation, not total output

close.condition: The candidate has found the forecast issue and looked upstream.

anchors.s9: Links "inventory up yet stockouts" to misallocation unprompted, finds both causes, and defends no-capex.
